verse.line: Suffering is born of worry, nothing else. Free of worry, you are happy and at peace.
verse.translation: One who knows for certain that suffering here is born of worry and nothing else is free of it, happy, at peace, and unattached everywhere.

verse.line: A ball knocked down bounces back up. For good people, setbacks rarely last.
verse.translation: A ball struck down by the hand flies right back up. As a rule, the misfortunes of those who live rightly do not last.

prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari tells the reader from his section on steadfastness. He speaks to someone who has been knocked down, comparing them to a ball struck by the hand. verse.scene_line: You are the ball, struck by the day, and still rising.

prasang.title: Vasishtha on self-effort: fate is only your past effort
prasang.summary: Vasishtha's first teaching to Rama is a long case for self-effort. What people call fate is simply the fruit of their own past effort, and present effort can overcome it, as the stronger of two rams wins. He also says not to torment yourself over what was beyond your power, and to steer your habits gently, like raising a child.
prasang.lesson: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha is speaking to Rama, who feels lost and blames his fate. Vasishtha tells him that what people call fate is just the result of past effort, and what they call effort is just future fate. The point is that your past effort built today, and your present effort builds tomorrow. You cannot change what was never in your hands, but you can steer your habits now to shape what comes next.
verse.for_you: You are holding the future like a weight in your hands, waiting for the work to turn out a certain way before you will rest. The tiredness is not just the care. It is the refusal to let the effort be enough. Today, let the work be the work.

story.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
story.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
story.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

verse.speaker: Draupadi
verse.setting: Draupadi argues that waiting on fate is no plan: people must act.
verse.sanskrit: कुर्वतो नार्थसिद्धिर्मे भवतीति ह भारत / निर्वेदो नात्र गन्तव्यो द्वावन्तौ यस्य कर्मणः
verse.line: Don't despair because effort hasn't paid off yet. Every attempt can go either way.
verse.translation: 'I keep working and still don't succeed' is no reason to despair. Every effort can end two ways, in success or not; only by not acting is the outcome certain.
verse.why: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

prasang.title: Do right without reward, and keep working
prasang.summary: Draupadi questions a world where the good suffer; Yudhishthira answers that he does right because it is right, not for reward. Draupadi replies that effort still matters: fate rewards no one who waits.
prasang.lesson: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

verse.meaning: Draupadi speaks to Yudhishthira in the forest. Yudhishthira is grieving, believing that because they have done right, they deserve an easy outcome. Draupadi argues that effort is not a guarantee. Every attempt can end in success or not. Only by refusing to act is the result certain. The verse proposes that you do right for its own sake, and then work as if everything depends on you. It asks you to act with skill and care, but to let go of the idea that the outcome is already decided by your virtue.
verse.for_you: Your part is the effort, not the outcome; work done well is already complete, whatever result comes.
verse.try_today: Notice one task done well, then step away without checking the result.
verse.scene_line: You are in the forest, waiting for a good outcome that your effort alone cannot promise.
asks: How do I do my work well without needing it to turn out a certain way?
What does it mean to act as if everything depends on me?

verse.speaker: Seer
verse.setting: Follows the call to enjoy by letting go: how to live and work.
verse.sanskrit: कुर्वन्नेवेह कर्माणि जिजीविषेच्छतꣳ समाः । एवं त्वयि नान्यथेतोऽस्ति न कर्म लिप्यते नरे ॥
verse.line: Do your work and wish to live a full hundred years. Done in this spirit, action does not cling.
verse.translation: Doing your work here, you may wish to live a hundred years. For you there is no other way than this: done in this spirit, action does not cling to a person.
verse.why: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

prasang.title: The Isha: enjoy by letting go
prasang.summary: Eighteen verses that open by saying everything belongs to the divine, so we should enjoy it without grasping. They go on to say we should work a full life without being bound, and see ourselves in all beings.
prasang.lesson: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

verse.meaning: The Seer speaks to the reader about how to live and work. They say you may wish to live a full hundred years doing your work here, but for you there is no other way than this. Done in this spirit, action does not cling to a person.
verse.for_you: The lists for work and for your parents never seem to end, and the mind stays restless because it wants the results to land a certain way before it can rest.
verse.try_today: Do one small task for your parents without deciding how it must end.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own long life, working and caring, with the outcome still open.
asks: How do I do the work without holding the outcome?
What does it mean for action to not cling to me?
Can I wish for a hundred years while I am this tired?

verse.speaker: Teacher
verse.sanskrit: आचार्याय प्रियं धनमाहृत्य प्रजातन्तुं मा व्यवच्छेत्सीः । सत्यान्न प्रमदितव्यम् । धर्मान्न प्रमदितव्यम् । कुशलान्न प्रमदितव्यम् । भूत्यै न प्रमदितव्यम् । स्वाध्यायप्रवचनाभ्यां न प्रमदितव्यम् ॥
verse.line: Do not drift from truth or duty. Do not neglect your wellbeing, your prosperity, or your learning.
verse.translation: Having brought your teacher the gift he values, do not cut off the line of your family. Do not drift from truth. Do not drift from what is right. Do not neglect your wellbeing. Do not neglect your prosperity. Do not neglect study and teaching.
verse.why: Truth, right action, gratitude and graceful giving: a whole life in one speech.

prasang.title: The graduation address
prasang.summary: As a student finishes his studies and leaves to start family life, the teacher gives him parting instructions: speak truth, do right, keep learning, honour mother, father, teacher and guest, give with grace. He even tells the student to copy only the teachers' good conduct, and when in doubt to act as thoughtful, gentle people would.
prasang.lesson: Truth, right action, gratitude and graceful giving: a whole life in one speech.

verse.meaning: The teacher is speaking to a student who has just finished his studies and is about to leave. He is giving final instructions for the life ahead. He says do not drift from truth. Do not drift from what is right. Do not neglect your wellbeing. Do not neglect your prosperity. Do not neglect study and teaching. He is reminding the student that a whole life rests on these things. The work is not just about getting ahead or surviving. It is about staying true to the path while also caring for the self.
verse.for_you: You are standing at a point where the work and the care for your parents pull in different directions. The mind wants to settle on a single outcome, but the days keep moving. This verse asks you to hold the work and the care as part of one whole life.
verse.try_today: Before you rest, name one thing you did today that was right, not just productive.

story.title: Hanuman's search and near despair
story.story_hook: Hanuman had searched every palace in Lanka by moonlight, and she was nowhere.
story.summary: Hanuman searches Lanka all night without finding Sita. He is close to despair, weighing what failure will mean for everyone, then tells himself that refusing to lose heart is the root of success, and searches again.
story.lesson: When you have looked everywhere, look again; giving up costs too much.

anchor.speaker: Hanuman
anchor.setting: Unable to find Sita, Hanuman considers giving up altogether, then chooses to keep going.
anchor.sanskrit: विनाशे बहवो दोषा जीवन् प्राप्नोति भद्रकम्। तस्मात् प्राणान् धरिष्यामि ध्रुवो जीवति संगमः॥
anchor.line: Giving up costs too much. Whoever keeps going finds good things again.
anchor.translation: Giving up brings many harms; one who lives on finds good things. So I will hold on to life; for the living, meeting again is certain.
anchor.why: When you have looked everywhere, look again; giving up costs too much.
anchor.misuse: Hanuman is rejecting despair; anyone in crisis should reach out to someone right away.

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: Ashtavakra presses home his core teaching to Janaka: you are awareness, not the roles you play.
verse.sanskrit: गुणैः संवेष्टितो देहस्तिष्ठत्यायाति याति च । आत्मा न गन्ता नागन्ता किमेनमनुशोचसि ॥
verse.line: The body comes and goes; what you truly are does not. Why grieve so?
verse.translation: The body, made of nature's qualities, comes, stays and goes. The Self neither comes nor goes. Why grieve for it?
verse.why: You are the ocean, not the waves; let them rise and fall without losing yourself.
verse.misuse: Grief is natural; this offers perspective, not a rule against mourning.

prasang.title: You are not your mind
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra drives home that Janaka is not the body, the doer, or the mind's likes and dislikes, but the ocean in which the waves of life rise and fall. He urges faith, an end to grief, and rest from endless deliberation.
prasang.lesson: You are the ocean, not the waves; let them rise and fall without losing yourself.

verse.meaning: Ashtavakra tells Janaka that the body is born, it stays for a time, and it dies. It is made of changing qualities. But the Self is not like that. The Self neither arrives nor leaves. It simply is. So why do you mourn for something that was never truly yours to lose?
verse.for_you: Your mind is caught in the coming and going of days, of work, of worry. You feel the weight of what might happen next. But you are not the one who must hold it all. You are the space in which these worries move, not the worries themselves.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment today when you are not the doer, only the space around it.
verse.scene_line: You are the stillness in which the body and its tasks rise and fall.
asks: How can I tell the difference between my thoughts and the space they move in?
Can I let the outcome go without letting go of the work?

verse.speaker: Rama
verse.setting: Rama, ending his questions, asks for one practical skill.
verse.sanskrit: व्यवहारवतो युक्त्या दुःखं नायाति मे यया । अथवा व्यवहारस्य ब्रूत तां युक्तिमुत्तमाम् ॥
verse.line: Teach me how to keep working in the world without the work filling me with sorrow.
verse.translation: Tell me the skill by which sorrow doesn't come to me while I go about my work, or else tell me the best way of dealing with life itself.
verse.why: The real question isn't whether to quit life, but how to live it without being swallowed.

prasang.title: Rama asks how to live in the world without being crushed by it
prasang.summary: After his lament Rama turns to questions. How did King Janaka and others stay free while running kingdoms? How can a person work in the world untouched, like water on a lotus leaf? He asks for one practical skill that lets him work without sorrow.
prasang.story_hook: Having said what was wrong, Rama finally asked the question that matters: how do the wise do it?
prasang.lesson: The real question isn't whether to quit life, but how to live it without being swallowed.

verse.for_you: Your part is the effort, not the outcome; work done well is already complete, whatever result comes.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how the wise live and work.
verse.sanskrit: यदृच्छालाभसन्तुष्टो द्वन्द्वातीतो विमत्सरः । समः सिद्धावसिद्धौ च कृत्वापि न निबध्यते ॥
verse.line: Content with what comes, beyond envy, steady in success and failure, you stay free even while working.
verse.translation: Content with whatever comes unasked, beyond the pairs of opposites, free from envy, the same in success and failure, even when acting he is not bound.
verse.why: Contentment and freedom from envy let you work without being bound.

prasang.title: How the great yogis live
prasang.summary: The wise act without selfish motive, content and dependent on nothing, free from envy, steady in success and failure.
prasang.lesson: Contentment and freedom from envy let you work without being bound.

verse.meaning: Krishna tells Arjuna that the wise person is content with whatever comes unasked and free from envy. They remain steady in success and failure, and even while acting, they are not bound. This is not about stopping work. It is about working without being chained to the result, keeping the inner self separate from the outer doing.
verse.for_you: Your mind will not settle because you are trying to hold the outcome before it happens. The teaching is to do the work and let the result go, to be steady in success and failure. You are not the work. You are the one who stands apart from it.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment when you do a task without checking the result.
verse.scene_line: You are working, but your mind is holding the result before it comes.
asks: How do I let the work go without it falling apart?
What does it mean to be steady when I am tired?
Can I rest while the work is still open?

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
verse.sanskrit: स्वाराज्ये भैक्षवृत्तौ च लाभालाभे जने वने । निर्विकल्पस्वभावस्य न विशेषोऽस्ति योगिनः ॥
verse.line: Throne or begging bowl, gain or loss, crowd or solitude: a steady person stays the same.
verse.translation: For the yogi of steady nature there is no difference between ruling a kingdom and living on alms, gain and loss, the crowd and the forest.

words.en: of the one with undoubting nature

verse.why: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

prasang.title: The calm of the wise
prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.
prasang.lesson: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

verse.meaning: Janaka, the king who sits on a throne, has asked how to live in the world without being swallowed by it. Ashtavakra tells him that the wise person does not move between places to find peace. The same calm that sits on a throne sits in a begging bowl. The same mind that does not break under gain does not break under loss. The same ease is found in a crowded city and in a silent forest. The difference is not in the chair or the bowl but in the one who holds them.
verse.for_you: The work and the care for your parents are your throne and your forest. You do not need to run from one to the other to find rest. The same mind that holds the work can hold the care. The same breath can move through both.
verse.try_today: Feel the difference between the task and the one who does it.
verse.scene_line: You sit with your parents in the quiet of the evening, and the work is still in your hands.
asks: How do I hold the work and the care without one swallowing the other?

verse.speaker: Teacher
verse.setting: Rules of conduct for a renunciant.
verse.sanskrit: नात्यर्थं सुखदुःखाभ्यां शरीरमुपतायेत् । स्तूयमानो न तुषेत निन्दितो न शपेत्परान् ॥
verse.line: Don't wear out your body chasing pleasure or fleeing pain. Praised, don't gloat; blamed, don't curse others.
verse.translation: Let him not torment the body too much for the sake of pleasure or pain. Praised, let him not gloat; blamed, let him not curse others.

If someone praises you, do not let it swell your chest. If someone blames you, do not turn that blame into a weapon against others.
verse.for_you: The body comes and goes. What you truly are does not. Praised, don't gloat. Blamed, don't curse others.
verse.try_today: Pause before reacting to a slight or a win today.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse.sanskrit: नेहाभिक्रमनाशोऽस्ति प्रत्यवायो न विद्यते । स्वल्पमप्यस्य धर्मस्य त्रायते महतो भयात् ॥
verse.line: No sincere effort here is ever wasted. Even a little of it shields you from great fear.
verse.translation: On this path no effort is lost and no harm results. Even a little of this practice protects one from great fear.

words.en: here no stepping back, no destruction

verse.why: Do the work fully; let go of owning the result.

prasang.title: The yoga of action
prasang.summary: Krishna teaches the yoga of action: work wholeheartedly, give up clinging to outcomes, stay even in success and failure, and keep a single steady purpose.
prasang.lesson: Do the work fully; let go of owning the result.

verse.meaning: Krishna is telling Arjuna that no effort put into doing what is right is ever lost. Even a small step on this path is enough to guard against great fear. The point is to give the work your full attention, but to let go of owning the result. The work itself is the practice, and the result is not yours to keep.
verse.for_you: The work with your parents and your job demands your full attention, but the result is not yours to own. The rest you need comes from letting go of the outcome. Your part is the effort, not the final shape of things.
verse.try_today: Notice the work itself, not the outcome it will bring.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own waiting room, and the work is not lost.
asks: How do I let go of the outcome?
How can I rest without knowing the result?

story.title: Pingala's song: the night she stopped waiting
story.story_hook: Pingala sat awake listening for footsteps that never came, until she stopped listening.
story.summary: Pingala waited all night for a lover who never came. At last she saw that her peace depended on someone else's arrival, let the expectation go, and slept peacefully.
story.lesson: Letting go of an expectation can bring the sleep that waiting never will.

anchor.setting: Pingala, left waiting all night by a lover who never came, finally lets go and finds peace.
anchor.sanskrit: सुखं निराशः स्वपिति नैराश्यं परमं सुखम् / आशामनाशां कृत्वा हि सुखं स्वपिति पिङ्गला
anchor.line: Pingala let go of her expectation and slept peacefully. Letting go of expectation is the greatest ease.
anchor.translation: The one free of expectation sleeps in peace; freedom from expectation is the highest happiness. Turning hope into no-hope, Pingala sleeps peacefully.
